newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Communists do well in polls, Kremlin stays calm.
newsitem.headline: Communists do well in polls, Kremlin stays calm.

text.p: Russia's opposition communists defeated President Boris Yeltsin's camp in a string of weekend elections for regional governors, results showed on Monday.

But presidential aides shrugged off the setbacks, which gave the opposition four outright wins to the Kremlin's two in Sunday's voting, saying the Kremlin could work smoothly with most of the opposition winners.
"We will take all necessary steps to find a common language with the elected governors," Alexander Kazakov, Yeltsin's deputy chief-of-staff, told Itar-Tass news agency.

Candidates from the communist-led Union of National and Patriotic Forces swept the governorships in four of the 10 regions which voted, with seats in Russia's upper house of parliament the main prize.
Opposition candidates are also favourites in two regions where a run-off will be needed because no candidate won enough votes for outright victory on Sunday.
Candidates openly backed by Yeltsin's administration won in two regions and have good chances of winning run-off votes in two other regions where a run-off will be required.

Elections will have been held for governors in 52 of Russia's 89 regions by the end of the year. Regional governors make up half the seats in the Federation Council upper house, the other half of which are occupied by regional council heads.

The communist-led opposition has a majority in the State Duma, the lower house. It says the voting so far, which already covers 40 of the 52 regions which will vote, puts them well on the way to gaining control of the Federation Council.
Liberals say the score is much closer and Kazakov said the Kremlin saw no real problems in dealing with all but one communist governors.
"A clear-cut opposition candidate won only in Bryansk region," he said, referring to communist Yuri Lodkin, the new governor of the traditionally conservative western region.
"Elsewhere normal, reasonable people who have a solid experience in running the local economy came to power."
Statements by some communist winners seemed to give the Kremlin reason for optimism.

Yuri Guskov, who trailed the local pro-Yeltsin governor in Sunday's first round of voting in Arkhangelsk, made clear he would cooperate with the government if he won the run-off vote in the norther region.
The Kremlin appears more worried by the growing independence of regional governors than by their political preferences.

Until now, most regional governors were appointed and sacked directly by Yeltsin. They often acted on Yeltsin's behalf in local conflicts and as Moscow's emissaries in pushing though unpopular government decisions.
The polls that are under way mark a big change. Governors will now depend more on their voters than on the Kremlin and could turn into lobbyists in Moscow for their regions.

In a country where wage delays have grown into a national problem, and where a lack of tax revenues prevents the cabinet from carrying out its budget obligations to the regions, this change may cause huge problems for the Kremlin.

The first sign of fresh headaches came last week, when angry members of the Federation Council blasted Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin for ignoring pleas to come to address them. Some sugegsted initiating a no-confidence vote in the government.
